Pilar 3 on real data — 4D NDVI forecasting with sequential Bayesian assimilation

Hugo Rodrigues

Source: vignettes/articles/pilar3-4d-real.Rmd
pilar3-4d-real.Rmd

1. Why this vignette exists

The original Pillar 3 vignette (vignette("pilar3-4d-soc")) demonstrates the stacked ConvLSTM (Shi et al. 2015) on the synthetic SOC cube produced by temporal_synth_soc_cube(). As of v1.5.0 the Pillar 3 story runs on real Cerrado spatio-temporal data: 168 monthly time steps (January 2010 – December 2023) of three channels assembled over a 2° × 2° AoI centred on the Goiás / Minas Gerais triple-junction (lon –48 to –46, lat –16 to –14, 10 × 10 = 100 cells at 0.2° resolution):

  1. NDVI from MODIS MOD13Q1 250 m 16-day composites aggregated to monthly means (Didan 2015) — the forecast target.
  2. Monthly precipitation (mm/month) from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 bias-corrected) monthly mean daily totals (Stackhouse Jr. et al. 2018; Sparks 2018). We originally targeted CHIRPS 0.05° (Funk et al. 2015) but the Climate Hazards Group data portal was returning HTTP 403 for every v2.0 global_monthly/tifs/ request at the v1.5.0 freeze; POWER is a fully-open NASA alternative with comparable accuracy over the Cerrado and a single-point REST API that returns the full 14-year series in one call.
  3. Mean monthly air temperature (°C) from NASA POWER T2M (Stackhouse Jr. et al. 2018), fetched in the same REST call as the precipitation. (We originally targeted WorldClim 2.1 static climatology (Fick and Hijmans 2017) but the geodata.ucdavis.edu server was in maintenance at the v1.5.0 freeze; POWER T2M has the added benefit of being year-specific rather than a long- term average, so all three channels now carry genuine year-to- year climate variability.)

The vignette also demonstrates the v1.5.0 new function temporal_kalman_update(): a stochastic Ensemble Kalman Filter (Evensen 1994; Burgers et al. 1998) that sequentially assimilates new in-situ observations into the ConvLSTM forecast without retraining the network.

The results in this article have been withdrawn. They need $obs, $scaling, $truth_future from temporal_cerrado_results.rds, which were removed on 2026-08-28 because they carried observed values at named coordinates. The package can no longer reproduce the forecast and assimilation figures, so the article stops here rather than display numbers that nothing in it backs. See PROVENANCE.md and data-raw/build/stripped_elements.csv in the repository.

Burgers, Gerrit, Peter Jan van Leeuwen, and Geir Evensen. 1998. “Analysis Scheme in the Ensemble Kalman Filter.” Monthly Weather Review 126 (6): 1719–24. https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1998)126<1719:ASITEK>2.0.CO;2.
Didan, Kamel. 2015. MOD13Q1 MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 250 m SIN Grid V006. NASA EOSDIS Land Processes DAAC. https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD13Q1.006.
Evensen, Geir. 1994. “Sequential Data Assimilation with a Nonlinear Quasi-Geostrophic Model Using Monte Carlo Methods to Forecast Error Statistics.” Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans 99 (C5): 10143–62. https://doi.org/10.1029/94JC00572.
Fick, S. E., and R. J. Hijmans. 2017. “WorldClim 2: New 1-Km Spatial Resolution Climate Surfaces for Global Land Areas.” International Journal of Climatology 37 (12): 4302–15. https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.5086.
Funk, Chris, Pete Peterson, Martin Landsfeld, et al. 2015. “The Climate Hazards Infrared Precipitation with Stations — a New Environmental Record for Monitoring Extremes.” Scientific Data 2: 150066. https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2015.66.
Shi, X., Z. Chen, H. Wang, D.-Y. Yeung, W.-K. Wong, and W.-C. Woo. 2015. “Convolutional LSTM Network: A Machine Learning Approach for Precipitation Nowcasting.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28: 802–10.
Sparks, Adam H. 2018. “nasapower: A NASA POWER Global Meteorology, Surface Solar Energy and Climatology Data Client for R.” Journal of Open Source Software 3 (30): 1035. https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.01035.
Stackhouse Jr., Paul W., David Westberg, James M. Hoell, William S. Chandler, and Taiping Zhang. 2018. NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) — Release 8 methodology. NASA Langley Research Center.
